acceptedAnswer.text: Freight rework is the corrective handling that returns a load to a deliverable state: freight that shifted in transit, a load a receiver refused at the dock, damaged or collapsed pallets, and overweight or axle-illegal loads are unloaded under control, sorted, restacked, repalletized, re-wrapped and re-secured — with the damage separated and documented — so the truck can deliver or legally roll. The Flat Rate Movers performs freight reworks and load-shift corrections from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV, at the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard — wherever the job requires.

mainEntity.name: My load shifted on the road. What happens now?

acceptedAnswer.text: Call +1-540-422-2153. Intake records what happened, where the truck is and what the freight is — photos of the load as it sits speed the quote. The job is scoped and quoted at one flat rate before work begins. At the site, the trailer is opened under control because a shifted load can fall at the doors; the load is photographed as found, counted against the bill of lading, unloaded in sequence, restacked and repalletized, reloaded in delivery sequence, and secured so the tiedowns' aggregate working load limit reaches at least half the cargo weight, the federal standard in 49 CFR 393.106(d). You leave with after-photos, final counts and bill-of-lading notation of the work.

mainEntity.name: A receiver refused my load. Can you rebuild it for redelivery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Refused and rejected loads are a core part of this service: leaning or collapsed pallets are rebuilt, freight is restacked to the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, mixed product is sorted to specification, damaged cases are pulled and documented, and counts are verified against the bill of lading. The rebuilt load is photographed and signed for at hand-back, so the redelivery arrives as documented.

mainEntity.name: Can you correct an overweight or axle-weight problem?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Axle correction is part of the rework scope: freight is repositioned along the box, redistributed between the steer, drive and tandem axles, partially offloaded and reloaded, or split across equipment, so the truck can legally roll — verified against the scale ticket where a scale is part of the job.

mainEntity.name: Do you repalletize freight to a receiver's specification?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Rebuilding to the receiver's specification is the point of the work: sound pallets of the required type, the receiver's Ti/Hi pattern and stack height, failed packaging replaced where needed, and the load re-wrapped and secured. Floor-loaded freight is also palletized to specification for receivers that accept palletized freight only.

mainEntity.name: What documentation comes with a rework?

acceptedAnswer.text: Photographs of the load as found before it is touched, counts against the bill of lading at unload and at reload, specific damage exceptions written on the delivery paperwork, after-photos of the rebuilt load, bill-of-lading notation of the work performed, and receiver or carrier sign-off at hand-back. The record is built to support the OS&D report and any cargo claim that follows — a clean signature with unnoted damage is the carrier's best evidence against a claim, so exceptions are written at the dock, while the driver is present.

Nothing is auto-priced and hourly pricing is available when a client asks for it. Photos of the load as it sits speed the intake. Emergency and after-hours work is quoted at the emergency premium. mainEntity.name: Is emergency or after-hours rework available?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Emergency and after-hours response for shifted, refused and axle-held loads is available, at premium rates. A load standing still is burning detention and a driver's hours; call +1-540-422-2153 and the intake starts with where the truck is and what the freight is.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between cross-docking, transloading and rework?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rework fixes the freight: the load cannot deliver as it sits, and the corrective work returns it to a deliverable, legal, secured state. Cross-docking moves the freight: inbound freight is unloaded and transferred directly onto outbound vehicles, sorted and consolidated dock to dock, typically turned in under 24 hours with little to no storage — best for high-velocity goods, retail distribution, e-commerce and perishables. Transloading changes the mode: freight moves between transportation modes — ocean container or railcar to domestic truck — and may be repalletized, sorted or held in short staging during the switch — best for long-distance international shipping, intermodal networks and bulk or heavy goods. A rework can be inserted into either operation when freight arrives wrong.

The company works rail-served spots when contracted: at a rail-served location, the transfer chain runs railcar arrival and inbound checks, unload, staging or sorting in the transfer area, and outbound truck loads built for the delivery leg, with counts taken at every touch so the inventory record survives the mode change. The company claims no owned rail siding or railroad authority; the work is contracted transfer work at the facility's location.

Wherever the job requires: the company's leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. Dispatch runs from both branches — The Flat Rate Movers in Winchester, VA and Flat Rate Movers Martinsburg WV — across the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridors; the two branches are distinct, with their own addresses, hours and service areas.

mainEntity.name: Who pays for unloading and rework labor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under federal law, the shipper or receiver is financially responsible for loading and unloading assistance — 49 USC 14103 — not the driver; a driver who pays at the dock is reimbursed on the receipt, and the lumper fees charged at receivers typically run per load. The rework itself is quoted by this company at one flat rate before work begins; who ultimately bears that cost between shipper, carrier, broker and receiver is a matter for their contracts and any cargo claim.

Yes. Floor-loaded containers and trailers are unloaded piece by piece, counted and checked, and built onto pallets to the receiver's specification — the standard inland leg for container freight moving through the Virginia Inland Port chain and for imports that arrive floor-loaded.

Yes. Damaged freight is separated from good freight at the unload — crushed, torn or water-damaged cases are pulled, photographed and documented, never buried back into the load — so the deliverable part of the shipment can still deliver, and the damaged part carries the documentation an OS&D report and a cargo claim require.
